This paper introduces the Temporal-Varying Poisson Autoregression (TV-PAR) model, a flexible framework for modeling and forecasting univariate count time series. We begin by defining the model specification and deriving its spectral density. Subsequently, we summarize key theoretical contributions, which include practical guidelines for identification and estimation. To assess the model's finite-sample performance, we conduct extensive simulation studies comparing TV-PAR against existing time series models. Furthermore, we apply the model to real-world data to examine its spectral characteristics, spectral regularities, and forecasting capabilities. The results demonstrate that allowing autoregressive parameters to vary over time in a gentle, cyclic manner significantly enhances both the fit and forecasting accuracy. Finally, we outline potential future research directions for this work. The proposed methods are accessible via the R package tvpar (available at https://github.com/abhijit-1987/TVPAR).

The approach relies solely on the spectral decomposition of two-point correlation functions and the associated positivity constraints, requiring no assumptions about gauge symmetry, asymptotic freedom, or confinement. Utilizing the high-energy asymptotic fall-off of meson and baryon correlation functions as input, the method generates a nonperturbative spectrum based on these functions and their inherent positivity properties. By ensuring that the spectral density on the right-hand side of the decomposition adheres to physical hadronic spectra, a novel prediction is established for this spectrum. Applied to SU(2) and low-lying SU(3) mesons and baryons, the technique yields predictions for all unknown states up to approximately 3.2 GeV, contingent upon their asymptotic masses. When extended to higher masses, further spectral data is required for prediction; for instance, forecasting the number of SU(3) baryons at 2.7 GeV utilizes a basis of correlation functions derived from mesons and baryons with masses of 2.7 GeV, 3.0 GeV, and 3.2 GeV. Furthermore, this framework offers predictions for hadronic states at any specified mass when sufficient lower-mass hadronic data is available, and it remains applicable to any flavor group, such as SU(4). We provide explicit mathematical formulations for all necessary steps, supplying a complete recipe for fitting a PDF within any specific model. To implement this approach practically, we have developed a Monte Carlo integration code named "SHAPE" (Shapecode for Monte Carlo Integration for Parton Distribution Function Evolution). We conclude the review by outlining several key challenges that must be addressed to secure the long-term success of this methodology. Nonlocal gravity (NLG) represents a hereditary theory of gravity characterized by a constitutive relationship between nonlocal tensor quantities and local tensors. This paper provides a concise overview of the NLG framework, emphasizing its constitutive equation and the associated constitutive connection. The author outlines potential applications of NLG, including modeling the gravitational collapse of neutron stars, analyzing the dynamical stability of compact objects, and exploring cosmological phenomena. While a comprehensive exploration of the constitutive connection's properties and characteristics exceeds the scope of this review, a specific form of NLG utilizing a simple constitutive relationship is examined to investigate these attributes. Ultimately, the feasibility of constructing a nonlocal gravity model with an arbitrary constitutive connection is discussed. Comparative analyses are drawn between NLG and other nonlocal theories, such as nonlocal elasticity, and between the constitutive connection in NLG and the Einstein-Ainstein infeld-Laubereil connection. Additionally, the relationship between the constitutive connection and the Riemann tensor in NLG is examined in light of a recent claim regarding the existence of a Riemann tensor defined with the constitutive connection in this framework.

Utilizing this approach, we determine the contextual correctness of several well-known semantic properties, including gradual typing, type systems for gradual languages, and type systems for programming languages. As an application, we employ the framework to derive metrics for type systems, assessing the "quality" of a type system $T$ by measuring the distance between $T$ and an ideal type system $\Omega$ that encompasses only structural rules. As anticipated, we demonstrate that this metric satisfies a triangle inequality and that specific type system designs correspond to expected distances relative to $\Omega$. Furthermore, we illustrate how this metric can guide the selection of a type system with the smallest distance from $\Omega$ in a multi-type system scenario. We conclude by outlining potential directions for extending this framework. The proposed methodology provides a rigorous metric-based framework for analyzing type systems, with broad implications for the design, evaluation, and optimization of type systems and languages, as well as for establishing quality standards. The defined metric between properties could also serve as a foundation for optimizing trade-offs among multiple semantic properties in the development of programming language features. Additionally, the framework offers precise measures for the semantic impact of code changes, facilitating the semantic-based optimization of compiler optimizations and guiding semantic property-based semantic integration during language evolution. The defined metric between contexts could likewise support optimizing context switching in polytypic programming and generating semantically optimal foreign function interfaces when invoking code written in different languages.

This study introduces a step-wise, exact method for detecting damage formation in self-sensing composites through electrical impedance tomography (EIT). Unlike traditional EIT approaches that rely on fitting physics-informed neural networks to invert material properties for damage identification, the proposed exact method utilizes genetic algorithms (GA). Specifically, GA determines the formation and location of cracks by optimizing two variables: the coordinates of crack vertices and the number of cracks, targeting specific electro-mechanical signatures. The efficacy of this exact approach is verified against a finite element model and compared with the industry-standard EIT neural network method. Results demonstrate that the exact method precisely identifies both the coordinates and the count of multiple cracks, achieving superior accuracy over the neural network approach. Consequently, this study confirms that genetic algorithms serve as an effective alternative to neural networks for damage detection in self-sensing composites, offering an exact solution that enhances detection accuracy without introducing the approximation errors typical of neural network models. Ultimately, this research highlights the potential of the GA-based exact method for real-time damage detection in self-sensing composite structures. Furthermore, the study presents a hybrid optimization strategy combining GA and gradient-based algorithms to reduce computational costs, validating the method's feasibility for real-time implementation in carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) health monitoring via electro-mechanical signature analysis. The proposed exact method and its optimized variant provide a robust framework for damage detection in self-sensing composites, potentially advancing their application in safety-critical industries such as aerospace and automotive sectors. Although focused on detecting crack coordinates and quantity, the framework is versatile and can be adapted for other damage-related tasks, including severity detection and classification in composite health monitoring. This study introduces a novel consistency regularization method designed to minimize the reliance on annotated data within semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The approach utilizes a variance-based consistency loss, derived from a probability distribution over segmentation maps generated by an ensemble of neural networks. These distributions are modeled using a simple two-layer mixture model. The network is trained via a end-to-end framework that incorporates an anatomically plausible adversarial loss. Furthermore, the integration of variance-based and adversarial losses significantly enhances segmentation quality compared to using either loss function independently. Additional benefits include improved robustness against noise in supervised labels and better performance with fewer annotated images. A key advantage of this end-to-end consistency regularization strategy is its universal applicability across various unsupervised learning tasks in medical image segmentation, such as domain adaptation.
